DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
## What the study claims

The study asks Cabinet to approve a district-wide weekly food waste collection from April 2027. It rests on four claims:
- **Strong pilot results.** The six-month pilot in 4,000 households showed strong participation.
- **One service for all.** Participation was similar in houses and flats, so one uniform service will work everywhere.
- **Local treatment.** Food waste will be treated at Brookfield, 14 miles away, saving £74 a tonne against incineration.
- **Fully funded.** The net cost of about £490,000 is covered by a provisional £520,000 new-burdens allocation.

I checked each claim against the study's own tables.

## Summary

Most of the arithmetic is correct, and some of the pilot's results are genuinely good: contamination is low and satisfaction is high. But three of the four claims above are contradicted by the study's own figures:
1. **Flats participation.** Flats participated at **21%**, against **66%** for houses. That is not "broadly similar."
2. **Tonnage.** The projection uses a **64%** participation rate that doesn't appear anywhere in the pilot data, so it overstates tonnage by roughly 13–15%.
3. **Capacity.** Brookfield can take only **1,800 tonnes** a year, but the study projects **3,290**. The disposal saving assumes all of it goes to Brookfield.

Once these are corrected, the service is no longer shown to be fully funded.

## 1. Arithmetic that checks out

- **Pilot participation:** 2,112/3,200 = 66%, 168/800 = 21%, and 2,280/4,000 = 57%.
- **Average yield:** the weighted average across houses and flats is 1.86 kg, which rounds to the stated 1.9 kg.
- **Projected tonnage:** 52,000 × 64% × 1.9 kg × 52 weeks = 3,288 tonnes, matching the stated 3,290.
- **Disposal saving:** £112 − £38 = £74 a tonne, and £74 × 3,290 tonnes = £243,000.
- **Vehicles:** £990,000 depreciated over 7 years = £141,400.
- **Crews:** 6 crews × 2 operatives × £34,000 = £408,000.
- **Totals:** costs sum to £733,400, and £733,400 − £243,000 = £490,400 net.

## 2. Flats are not "broadly similar"

Flats participated at 21%, against 66% for houses, so flats were about a third as likely to take part. They also produced less waste per participating household (1.4 kg against 1.9 kg).

The study's conclusion that the service can roll out "without a separate approach for flats," and the author's statement that "participation held up across houses and flats," both contradict Table 1. The pilot shows the opposite: flats need a different approach, such as communal bins or different collection points. The district has about 10,400 flats.

## 3. The tonnage projection

The study applies a **64%** participation rate. The pilot's overall rate was 57%, and its house rate was 66%. No figure in the pilot is 64%.

The pilot had the same mix as the district, with 20% flats. Projecting each housing type at its own rate gives:

| | Households | Participation | kg per week | Tonnes per year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | about 2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | about 159 |
| **Total** | | | | **about 2,870** |

That is about 420 tonnes (13%) below the study's 3,290. Using 57% and 1.9 kg for all households gives about 2,930 tonnes, which is still well below.

## 4. Treatment capacity

The study's own text shows that Brookfield can take at most 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029. Even on the corrected projection, about 1,070 tonnes a year has nowhere local to go. On the study's own projection, the excess is about 1,490 tonnes.

The excess must either go to the plant 46 miles away, at an unknown gate fee plus the cost of hauling it, or be incinerated. Incinerating it would mean paying to collect food waste separately and then burning it anyway, with no saving.

The author's statement that "treatment is local" is true only for about 1,800 tonnes. The £243,000 saving assumes every tonne goes to Brookfield at £38.

## 5. Funding: not shown to be fully funded

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net annual cost | Against £520,000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Study as written | £243,000 | £490,400 | £29,600 headroom |
| Corrected tonnage, all at Brookfield (not possible, because of capacity) | about £212,500 | about £520,900 | about £900 short |
| 1,800 t at Brookfield, the rest incinerated | £133,200 | £600,200 | **about £80,000 short** |

The real figure lies somewhere between the last two rows. Where exactly depends on what the 46-mile plant would cost. The study has to settle that before it can claim the service is fully funded.

**Other funding questions:**
- **The allocation is provisional.** It has only been "indicated" by the Government. Cabinet should know what happens if the confirmed figure is lower.
- **Up-front capital.** Depreciation spreads the vehicle cost over seven years, but the £990,000 is due when the vehicles are ordered and delivered, around March 2027. Caddies are also an up-front cost. The study doesn't say how these will be financed, or whether new-burdens funding can be used for capital.

**Possible missing costs.** The author says every cost line is shown. I can't see:
- cover for crew leave and sickness;
- supervision and management;
- the dedicated phone line and web page;
- financing costs on the vehicles;
- a separate service for flats;
- haulage of the excess tonnage.

Liners are also unclear. The study mentions only a three-month supply, so it needs to say whether liners will be provided after that, since this can affect participation.

## 6. Implementation and legal deadline

**The timetable has no slack.** Vehicles are delivered in March for collections starting 5 April. Crews are recruited in February and trained in March. Caddies go to 52,000 households in the same month. A delivery delay of even a few weeks moves the start date. A contingency is needed, such as hired vehicles or a phased start.

**Check the legal deadline.** My understanding is that the Simpler Recycling rules required English councils to start weekly food waste collections from 31 March 2026, unless they qualify for a transitional arrangement. If so, an April 2027 start may already be late. The study should state the council's legal position.

## 7. Claims that hold up

- **Contamination under 2%** is a good result.
- **81% of surveyed households rated the service good or very good.** The study should give the survey response rate, since satisfied participants are more likely to reply.
- **Fewer missed-collection reports after month one** is encouraging.

One caution applies to these results generally. A January–June pilot may not show summer yields or how participation holds up once the service is no longer new.

## What is settled and what is open

**Settled by the study's own figures:**
- flats participation was about a third of houses' participation;
- the projection rests on a 64% rate that isn't in the data;
- projected tonnage exceeds Brookfield's capacity by roughly 1,100–1,500 tonnes;
- the disposal saving is therefore overstated.

**Open, and what would settle each:**

| Question | What would settle it |
|---|---|
| Treatment of the excess tonnage | A quote from the 46-mile plant, including haulage |
| Funding | Confirmation of the new-burdens allocation, its terms, and whether it can be used for capital |
| Flats service | Design and cost of a separate approach for flats |
| Full cost | A complete cost schedule, including cover, management, financing and contact handling |
| Legal deadline | The council's position under the Simpler Recycling rules |

## Recommendation

The service is a legal duty, so the decision is how to deliver it, not whether. The vehicle lead time is real, so Cabinet may reasonably authorise the vehicle order now. But it should not approve the service as evidence-based and fully funded on the current figures.

It should ask for a revised study with:
1. tonnage projected separately for houses and flats, using the pilot's own rates;
2. a treatment plan and cost for the tonnage Brookfield cannot take;
3. a separate service design for flats;
4. a complete cost and funding schedule, with capital and revenue shown separately;
5. a fallback if the April 2027 timetable or the funding allocation slips.
